title: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination, Part 3: Without Your Knowledge
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
series: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of living faith, which is cultivated through experience, determination, and embracing doubt rather than seeking certainty. This approach allows for a deeper connection to Buddhist teachings and tradition, as well as personal growth and liberation. By letting go of attachment to one's own understanding and embracing uncertainty, we can develop a more open and curious mind that ultimately leads to freedom.

sentences.text: Good morning, everybody.
I was moved and a little horrified by my grand entrance just then.
I was [unclear: "pumped in circumstance"].
It made me feel like I must have something really important to tell you, so I hope that's true.
Well, first off, happy Rohatsu, everybody.
Today is December the 8th, the day in Japanese Buddhism when the enlightenment of the Buddha is celebrated.
She's not here right now, but I've been happy to have Ray Green around, who studied enough Japanese to know it's actually pronounced a little more like Rohatsu.
Ask her what day it is if you see her.
She'll say it that way, very naturally.
It's lovely.
But it's a natural part of the transmission of Buddhism that we mispronounce everything.
And for good or ill, we're always translating and changing and modifying and adapting while trying to have some clue of what it is that we started with.
I'm so appreciating also, as I always do, the back and forth between Jeff and me when we get to co-lead these sesshin, alternating talks.
It's funny, it's one of the better things I do all year.
I always forget that's the case until we're in the middle of it again.
I don't know why.
I feel a little bad about that.
Like, wow, this is amazing.
Somehow we come up with much more than either of us could come up with individually.
And oftentimes an entire talk from the other person sprouts like a beautiful flower out of just a side remark from the previous person.
We took on this topic this week of great faith, great doubt, and great determination, knowing, I think, that neither of us really understands much about any of that, but trusting this process.
So hopefully these talks will be helpful.
But I'm enjoying the process of them again, including the great doubt that we have anything useful to say.
And is it about what we say anyway?
Or about this whole process, this whole mandala of practice?
I was out of the Zendo early this morning having meetings with people, so I was out during morning service.
It was so surprising and beautiful to be listening to morning service from the outside.
Usually you're in the middle of it.
Maybe the kitchen's been enjoying this the whole time.
And you all sound so beautiful in here.
So moving.
Your voices in harmony.
The big bell booming out.
Dogen's amazing little pile of teachings there in the Genjokoan essay, being proclaimed.
It's funny trying to chant that, isn't it?
Either you just chant it and don't worry about what it means, or you try to keep track of what it means.
Wait, wait, wait, what was that one?
And there's another one.
So I was thinking about Dogen.
I was also thinking about Dogen earlier in the day, at six, in the dark, when we chanted the verse for putting on the formal robes, the robe verse.
There's a little story in one of Dogen's essays called Shobaganzo Kesa Kodoku, on the spiritual merits of the Kesa, the robe.
And this kind of robe, I'm wearing the brown one.
So I looked it up and I thought you'd enjoy hearing how it was for Dogen when he first ever heard that verse.
This, by the way, is the sweet and energetic translation of Reverend Nierman from Shasta Abbey, who likes words like "wilst" and "thou."
I usually avoid him, but he popped up first on my search results, so I thought, well, why avoid him?
Let's love him.
It's not too florid, this one.
But it does start with "wilst."

*Wilst I was in [unclear: "Tsung China"] doing my training on the long bench in the meditation hall, I noticed that every morning following the striking of the wake-up block, the monks who sat up either side of me would raise their folded Kesa in a gesture of offering.
Raise it up, place it on top of their head, respectfully make gassho, and recite a verse to themselves.

What they were saying in that verse was, How great and wondrous is the robe of enlightenment, formless and embracing every treasure, I wish to unfold the Buddhist teaching that I may help all sentient beings to the other shore.*
A little different translation than ours.
*How great and wondrous is the robe of enlightenment, formless and embracing every treasure, I wish to unfold the Buddhist teaching that I may help all sentient beings to the other shore.*
Dogen goes on.
*On the occasion when I learned this, a feeling I have never experienced before welled up in me.
A joy filled my body to overflowing, tears of gratitude, stealing from my eyes, rolling down my cheeks, wet the collar of my robe.
The reason for this was that I had been reading the Agama scriptures shortly before, and I had seen this passage, in what they chanted, [unclear: "Unhumbly offering up"] the Kesa above one's head.
I was not clear about the ceremonial procedure.
Now I was personally witnessing it and was filled with such joy and worshipful admiration of being able to see manifest before me its deep intent.
When I was in my native land there had never been a teacher to instruct me in this, nor any good spiritual companion.
How could I not regret the days and years I had vainly spent and not grieved their passing?*
That guy was only 22 when he came to China.
*But upon hearing and seeing what was before me, I was able to rejoice because of some good deed done in my past lives.

If I had vaguely remained in my homeland, how could I possibly have sat shoulder to shoulder with the treasures of the Sangha who had received and actually donned the Kesa of the Buddha in the correct fashion?
My joy and sorrow were not unmixed as my myriad tears issued forth.
Then in silence I took a vow.
No matter how be I ever so incompetent, I will become the inheritor of this Buddha Dharma.

I will correctly transmit the true teaching, and out of pity for the sentient beings in my homeland, I will help them see and hear the teachings concerning the robe that the Buddhas and ancestors have genuinely transmitted to me.*
So that's the big power of these apparently little moments and verses and vows and rituals we do, from Dogen's point of view.
We're big on robes in Soto Zen.
Some places they require everybody to wear robes all the time, with a little lighter touch.
Sometimes Soto Zen is called the cult of cloth.
Have you ever heard that before?
And we do enact that cult by sewing our own ceremonial robes, the little bib-like one or the larger priest robe.
The cult of cloth.
And of course, the cloth is like everything.
It's just cloth.
It came from the fabric store.
That's true, on the one hand.
On the other hand, it's also a deep, deep miracle.
How could this be?
How could this even be?
It's wondrous.
And it really is.
Like, imbued with incredible power and possible benefit to all beings.
And the idea, though, is that this is true for everything.
This is true for absolutely everything.
There's nothing that's just ordinary.
Everything is extraordinary.
So that's maybe the spiritual power of our way of practicing.
It's not that we jump up and down and have huge, tremendous, incredible realizations, necessarily.
Although that could happen.
Nothing wrong with that.
But more like it gradually dawns on us that everything is this way.
It has these wondrous, deep qualities, beyond anything we could quite imagine or think about or talk about or say.
And our work is to remember that.
Not an intellectual kind of remembering, but a felt, experienced kind of memory.
A little bit like in the story of Buddha, when he remembers the day sitting under the rose apple tree as a boy, his father working in the fields with the farmers.
And he just felt it somehow.
The depth of his life.
The feeling of the breeze.
The fields before him.
Really experienced it.

Jeff and I have been contrasting a little bit this kind of gradual realization, gradual feeling, gradual understanding, which is characterized by our Soto school of Zen, with a more intense breakthrough model, which is a little more characterized with the Rinzai school.
And just to remind you that we are generalizing and simplifying a lot, using these two schools of Buddhism as straw men to knock down.
Because it's good to notice that we have these two qualities in us.
Part of us is content with our confusion, willing to let it slowly dawn on us that we weren't confused all along, even though we don't believe it yet.
And a part of us is not content at all, and wants to leave this [unclear: "sundry"] world behind and break through into a bigger reality.
These are both good.
These are both important.
And both so easily misunderstood, and both so easily can turn to the light or to the dark, to clarity or to confusion.
The more gradual approach, as I mentioned, you can just put it in park for quite a while.
Not much really happens of value to anybody.
You might look pretty good.
The danger of the more assertive approach is you can just hurt yourself, beating your head against the wall.
And oftentimes it's just a subtle little change in trajectory or approach, and you see, oh, that's how I could learn something.
That's how I could really change and grow in a way that would help me and help others.
It takes a lot of patience, taking another run at it.
And it can help a lot to receive a little good feedback from your dear Dharma friends and teachers.
Sometimes that feedback comes in the form of kind reminders, and you say, oh, thank you, good idea.
Other times it comes in the form of friction and pain, which we don't like so much.
But that also helps us to correct our course.
Our primary approach here, of course, is slow, quiet.
I was preparing these [unclear: "marks"].
I was about to put "gentle" on there.
Then I realized, well, that's not always your subjective experience.
It doesn't always feel so gentle.

But somehow the interaction between our conditioned self, this complex me who thinks this and thinks that and has these opinions and views and history and all that, and this open, vast possibility, sometimes actually has a lot of friction in it.
It rubs you wrong.
But who is the you that it's rubbing?
That's really the question.
We get focused on the friction.
How do I solve that?
People come to endless meetings.
We should do it this way, we should do it that way, to avoid some of this friction.
But actually it's the you in the middle that's being revealed and displayed.
And healed.
So it's hard to know the best approach to this.
We try stuff, we hang around, we learn from each other.
We trust our gut for a while, and then we realize our gut was wrong anyway, and we have a new gut.
And we have a lot of faith in a long arc process.
I was just thinking about the graph that includes these dips and valleys, dips and valleys.
When you're on your way down in a valley, it may look like this is not worth it, this isn't helping me, this isn't right for me.
When you're on your way up the mountain, you may think this is the best thing ever, I'm going to tell all my friends.
But neither is quite right.
Here's something Dogen said in a Dharma talk to his students about this process.
*An ancient has said, associating with a good person is like walking through mist and dew.
Though you will not become drenched, gradually your robes will become damp.
This means that if you become familiar with a good person you will become good yourself, without being aware of it.
In ancient times a boy attended Master [unclear: "Gute"], like a Zen master.
Without noticing what he was learning or when he was even practicing, this boy realized the way, because he had served as a personal attendant to a master who had been practicing for a long time.
Similarly, if you practice zazen for a long time you will suddenly clarify the great matter and will know that zazen is the true gate.*
Zazen is the true gate.
Suzuki Roshi really appreciated this saying that Dogen brought up.
And Dogen was referring to someone else.
So all these stories go back so far.
This idea of walking through mist and dew, he talks about it in much the same way somewhere in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind: that our way is like walking through the fog.
He landed in San Francisco, walking through the fog.
You're just walking along, doing your best to practice day after day, not really sure what it all means.
Suddenly you notice how wet you are.
In our little sangha brochure out in the lobby we have a quotation about this from Suzuki Roshi.
Pretty big type on the front, we wrote.
Maybe I did this.
*Our way is to practice one step at a time, one breath at a time, with no gaining idea.* That's the whole quote.
With advertising like that, it's a wonder that we have any members.
This is slow and endless and you don't get anything.
So that's our way.

These quotations of Suzuki Roshi that we get from Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, which was published in '71, and not always so, that Jeff was reading from yesterday, published I think in the early '90s: they're actually really heavily edited and cleaned up versions of what Suzuki Roshi actually said.
There's nothing wrong with that.
Also very normal in the Buddhist world, right?
Translating all the time.
The super fun thing is that eventually the San Francisco Zen Center released all the actual transcriptions word by word.
Which is hard to do, because it's hard to not accidentally fill in all the words that are left out to make good English.
So here's something that Suzuki Roshi said in 1970.
I don't know if it was exactly the basis for this particular quotation in our brochure, but similar.
If you hunt around you can find the source material.
Here's what he really said.
So it's kind of fun.
He said:
*So we should not involve in hasty idea of attainment.
We should not practice to achieve something, to attain something.
Step by step, appreciating, you know, our everyday life, day by day, step by step is our way.
When we cannot see what we are doing, where we are, it is useless, you know, to put ourselves in hard practice.*
Let's read that last sentence again.
*When we cannot see what we are doing, where we are, it is useless, you know, to put ourselves in hard practice.* So this is interesting, implying that we're not anti-hard practice.
Sometimes hard practice is a good choice.
Other times, not so much.
And the key seems to be, he's saying, some sort of clarity or developed intuition.
Now is the time to really turn up the energy, to really go for it.
Sit with a lot of vigor, study hard, set down some of my other distractions and entertainments, work strenuously with my resistance to all this, really have lots of faith in my great determination.
Other times, maybe even better not.
Have a rest.
Accept the invitation to go home for the evening.
Be measured.
Loping along, a slow marathon of life.
Can't sprint the whole time.
And just keep practicing, whether we see some subjective results or not.
Because oftentimes we don't really see what the results might be from this practice.
Here are some lines that jumped out at me when you were chanting the Genjokoan this morning:
*Do not suppose that what you attain becomes your knowledge and is grasped by your intellect.
Although actualized immediately, what is inconceivable may not be apparent.
Its emergence is beyond your knowledge.*
Do you notice that you said that?
You can't know.
I just said that.
He said that.
You can't know.
How do you feel about that?
You can't know.
But it's really useful that we have friends and colleagues and family, because maybe they can know.
Maybe they can see the reflection in the glow in your eyes, the way you hold your body, the tone of your voice, the choices you make, the way you are.
It's not uncommon for people to say, "Oh, I'm practicing away, but I don't really feel any different."
But my spouse says I'm a lot calmer.
Do you think that's right?
Could that be true?
So anyway, this debate between sudden and gradual approaches is actually thousands of years old already.
So maybe it's just time for it to surface again.
And maybe these three points, great faith, great doubt, great determination, are a nice model to look at the whole thing together.
But maybe in this gradual Soto side, we emphasize great faith, right?
Stepping along, step by step.
No attainment.
You can't have a lot of faith to keep going, if that's the case.
But faith needs determination too.
It's not a received faith, right?
It's lived faith.
A faith determined through experience, and manifested through our determination.
And this more intense approach, great determination, working hard with our practice, this needs faith.
This needs faith to work.
So it might be great doubt in the middle that is the pivot, the fulcrum of these two approaches that really reflect each other.
It's not like there's really one or the other.
You can't have one without the other.
Maybe they balance on this great doubt.
So maybe a kind of stretching ourselves with a healthy kind of curiosity and skepticism, and not being so sure we know what's called for right now.
Who we are.
Who she is or he is.
Not to be so certain of our predictions of what's happening next.
I really appreciate [unclear: "a just talk"] yesterday.
I felt like he was experientially walking us through his own experience of great doubt as he thought about that talk.
That's so moving to me.
How do you meet this unexpected life?
If you're paying attention, it's completely unexpected. [unclear: "A deer without a foot"] will walk in front of you.
You know this is important, and you do not know what it means.
Maybe it's like great doubt with a big D.
Big D doubt.
Curiosity, not knowing.
The quality of some energy to it.
How do I meet this?
How do I respond?
What is this?
What is it?
The word doubt also shows up in the famous Five Hindrances to Meditation, from early Buddhism.
And we may, whether we knew it or not, have been practicing all five of these these last few days.
Do you know what you've been doing?
Let's see what this teaching points to.
The five are, this is my wording, the five hindrances are desire, angry aversion, spacey aversion, restlessness and doubt.
Little D doubt.
Desire is any moment when you want things to be other than the way they are.
I wish the bell would ring.
Right?
This is desire.
This is a wish that things were other than the way they are right now.
Right now the bell is not ringing.
And somehow you think you can formulate this thought that makes some kind of sense, that the bell should be ringing.
This is delusion, right?
Pure and simple.
Straight up.
And a hindrance.
Angry aversion, or annoyed aversion.
Has this been true?
Has this been present?
Spacey aversion.
Sometimes that's translated as sloth and torpor.
It's different from just sleepiness.
Sleepiness in itself is not a problem, I don't think.
Somehow the way sleepiness can manifest is an aversion.
Just being asleep is okay.
You've got to get to the bottom of sleepiness before you can have any idea about waking up, right?
That doesn't make sense.
So sleepiness can be a teaching, but there's a kind of aversive spaciness: I am not here.
That's my plan.
My plan is to not be here.
My body may be here, but I am not here.
Maybe that will allow the first thing, that bell-ringing desire, to happen if I just check out.
This actually kind of works.
I'm sure you've tried it.
Restlessness needs no introduction.
This whole thing is designed to reveal the qualities of restlessness.
And little d, doubt.
This is pointless.
I'm no good at it.
Or, it depends on whether you put the locus of control for your craziness on the inside or the outside; it depends on how you express little d, doubt, right?
Internal control is like, "I'm no good at this," right?
Because of the outcome.
External control: "They're no good at this.
It's set up wrong here.
The teachings aren't right.
The schedule's not right."
Something I vaguely remember from some other event at some other Zen center fifty years ago.
That's how it should be.
If they knew that, then this would all be working much better.
That's little d, doubt.
So great doubt is not that.
It's big D, doubt.
And one way I think to distinguish is that there are very different qualities of suffering.
Sometimes we say in Zen, another reason why we have small groups, we say study your suffering.
Suffering is your teacher.
So the suffering of little d, doubt is very heavy.
Very discouraging.
Very dead.
The suffering and confusion of big D, doubt is alive, you know.
It's vital.
It's powerful.
You may not know what to do with it, but there's a sense of aliveness even as it may be mixed with discomfort, confusion, and any emotion you can think of.
It's all right there.
My current favorite expression for great doubt with a big D is "don't be so sure."
Don't be so sure.
And can we see the upside of this not being so sure, and not be too mired down by the downside?
The mind that wants to be sure is pretty frustrated.
But the mind that can release itself from needing to be so sure is liberated.
It's wide open.
So anyway, I think it's interesting to play with these ideas.
Please don't be too literal about it all, or worry too much if you've got it right, because that would put Jeff and me way on the spot.
We don't want that.
We don't think we're right.
Why would you think that?
It's a process of practice and exploration.
Investigation.
Based on something, I hope.
Every job in the Mondo is equally important, washing the dishes or giving the talk.
Although in both cases you put somebody in that job who has some experience, who knows how to wash a dish or has a little background to give a talk.
We don't expect dishes that never get dirty to come out of that process, right?
So why would you expect a perfect talk?
If everything is correct, I just have to figure it out.
That's the mind that wants to be so sure.
Maybe the best way to take these different kinds of teachings and phrases and expressions is to think about it more like optics.
Little mirrors or little lenses, just to give you another way to look at it.
I'm going to take this up and see what I see.
Because our usual view is pretty habitual, pretty habituated.
Gets a little narrow over the years.
So these are ways to expand our view and see ourselves a little differently.
So I want to return, to close my talk, to a little more about the history of Zen coming to America, these couple of figures that I'm so inspired by.
For time I'm going to say a little less than I was intending.
That's all right.
The two characters I was focused on are the teacher and the student.
The teacher is Sho Yanshaku.
The student I was focused on is Nyo Gen Senzaki.
Of course teachers become students, and we need to show our hand to keep track of these names that aren't so familiar.
The backstory in brief.
It's hard for me to do this in brief.
I'm attached to this story.
But I don't want to make your knees die.
Okay.

Sho Yanshaku was, for some reason we don't really know why, I think invited to a big international meeting in 1893 in Chicago about religion: the World Parliament of Religion, which is seen as a pivotal moment in American Zen history because we think it's the first talk given in America by an authorized Zen teacher about the Dharma.
Of course westerners have been exploring Buddhism for some hundreds of years before this too.
Anyway, Sho Yanshaku brought one student with him who is very familiar to us: Daitetsu Teiran Suzuki.
DT Suzuki.
And this is a younger student that I got interested in, Nyo Gen Senzaki, who briefly knew DT Suzuki when they were students in college.
In Sanskrit class, it turns out.
In Sanskrit class together.
Remember old professor so and so?
DT Suzuki stays in America in this trip that begins in 1893.
Stays for 11 years doing scholarly work.
He was the more scholarly of the two.
I don't know if they were really close friends, but we'll call them friends for convenience.
Two monks.
And Nyo Gen Senzaki is the more monkly, more oriented around practice.
Not so scholastic.
It actually kind of works to think of them as brothers, with Sho Yanshaku as the father.
We use that language around here a little bit, and it really was pretty true in the Zen monastic establishment, because the boys, and they were boys, left their families young.
You know, ordained at 10, 12, 13.
Sent off to live in a monastery, or living in their family monastery, literally.
Both Buddhist family and biological family mixed together in all kinds of ways.
And so DT Suzuki was the favorite son for sure, in this little family constellation.
We know in his journals Sho Yanshaku talked about DT Suzuki all the time.
He was so proud of his work and his books.
Hardly mentioned Nyo Gen Senzaki at all.
Nyo Gen Senzaki gets to America a little later.
In 1905, Sho Yanshaku was invited back to America by a wealthy industrialist named Alexander Russell, invited there to teach Zen in their household.
I was just trying to picture that, you know, getting a call from Bill Gates, who just released his annual list of books he liked this year, which included a book on meditation.
Did you know that?
Yeah.
And oddly, because of that, my fate is bound up in this.
I got an email from KUOW asking me to come talk about meditation.
So maybe Bill Gates did invite me.
Because the email from KUOW said, because Bill Gates.
So anyway, Sho Yanshaku in 1905 got a similar invitation.
I think in this case it was kind of the height of Orientalism.
It was popular in intellectual western circles to study the East, the mysterious East.
Which in some ways is wonderful, in some ways is outrageously racist in all kinds of strange ways.
So I don't know the character of Alexander Russell or what he did, but I imagine it would be a pretty cool thing with your friends to say, oh yeah, Zen Master living in my house.
That would be cool.
And probably they had him give talks in the living room and people came over, like salons.
But it was his wife who really got interested in Zen as a practice.
And I cannot find her first name so far.
She's always referred to as Mrs.
Alexander Russell.
If you know her name, let me know later.
Look for it.
It doesn't say how they practiced together, but it must be they had zazen and dokusan regularly, because she passed at least one koan in the formal Rinzai way of passing a koan.
May have been the first western person in history to do that.
Now lost to history as Mrs.
Alexander Russell.
And Nyogen Senzaki, the less important son, was in the household, but kind of working as a handyman.
Wasn't really included, apparently.
One of the few mentions of him in his teacher's journals was, let's see, I wrote down here somewhere.
I'm not seeing it right now, but it was something like, unfortunately Mr.
Nyogen Senzaki left the household as he was no longer able to do the handyman work.
Poor guy, you know, this Japanese monk, trying to picture him as so sincere.
And they had a famous parting, as I mentioned on Thursday, in a foggy park in San Francisco.
Which is not mentioned in the teacher's writings, but is mentioned in the student's writings.
In Nyogen Senzaki's writings, he quotes his teacher as saying, just face the great city and see whether it conquers you or you conquer it.
Do not feel obliged to serve me any longer.
And then they never see each other again, you know.
And Senzaki just finds his way in the big city.
Eventually teaching, and a little sangha forms around him.
Took many, many years, though.
Many, many years.
And then years later we know from his writings he did an annual memorial sesshin for his teacher, who died on November 1st, 1935.
Every year.
And there's a series of these translated in the book I have of his little talks.
I guess he probably gave the talks in English, but I don't know if he composed them in English or Japanese.
Devoted talks to his dear teacher.
And there's something so sad here, and also something so deep here about devotion.
I don't know if this is more part of the Japanese character, it seems like it, but I don't want to be another Orientalist in the 21st century.
I've only been to Japan for three weeks, you know.
But there's a feeling of devotion that really runs through the writings and the Japanese Buddhists that I've met.
Like one thing their teacher said to them one day, and how they thought about that for so many years.
And that you can be the devoted student of a teacher who may not have really emotionally returned that devotion in an overt way.
That in this way of practicing is not dishonest or making big of something that isn't real, but is in a way even more deep and even more important and even more real.
Even more pure.
So all the rest of his life, Nyogen Senzaki was devoted to his teacher, who may have forgotten all about him long ago.
Leaving him alone in America to find his way.
So one of the things he translates in these remarks, I want to close with, is a Dharma talk given by his teacher Shoyanshaku on December 8th, 1895.
Do you recognize the date there?
December 8th.
So this is a Rohatsu talk.
He gives a lovely little description of zazen, and he closes with the story of his own awakening.
I thought I would end with a kind of classic great determination enlightenment story.
Feel free to change your posture if you're getting uncomfortable.
It's been a little while.
Where does it start?
And a brief side note.
The other thing that's interesting about Shoyanshaku, Shoyanshaku, sorry, is after he completed his monastic training in Japan, he got interested in early Buddhism in his studies.
And he went off to Sri Lanka on his own to study with the Buddhists there, the Theravada Buddhists of Sri Lanka, in the 1880s.
He didn't speak any language that they had in common, but he just kind of found his way.
Learned what he could.
His teacher apparently didn't approve: you're supposed to be working in the temple now, buddy.
So that comes up in the story.
So this is Shoyanshaku, in 1895, on Rohatsu day.
*Years ago I was blown by karmic winds to the Indian Sea, where I moored in Ceylon for quite a while.
When I was to return to Japan I wanted to stop in Siam and observe Buddhism there.
I bought a ticket to Singapore but as I had no money to buy a cabin passage I had to take the deck space.
There were Chinese, Europeans and Negroes all grouped together.
We did not look upon each other with friendly eyes.
Our faces were bathed by the salt wind and our heads were washed with the rain.
I had no cushion to sit on and no space in which to stretch out.
With not enough bread or water, hunger and thirst brought me near to collapse.
No one seemed to notice that I was a human being.
I was like a sick dog.*
*Our boat reached the mouth of the Menom River at Bangkok but the tide was so low that our ship was grounded.
We had to remain on the ship one more night at the river's mouth.
I did not realize at the time that this was going to happen, and it would prove to be the test of my zazen powers.
It was towards evening and black clouds closed down over the four corners of the world.
The air pressure was becoming heavier and heavier.
Was it rain?
No.
Was it wind?
No.
It was just the heat rising like steam.
Sweat washed over my entire body.
Suddenly countless mosquitoes attacked from front and back, left and right.

*When evening came and everyone went to sleep there was no sound.
The engines were quiet and the only light came from the side lantern.

The army of mosquitoes then increased greatly, coming and going busily.
I chased them with my hands.
Then they went to my feet.
If I moved my feet they went to my face.
Some of them camped on my back.
I could not reach them.
I suffered beyond all words.
At that time I thought to myself, in olden times bodhisattvas forgot their own bodies to save others, even willing to lose their lives for the sake of the teaching.
Someone cut off his arms while standing in the snow.
Someone pierced his thigh with a sharp gimlet to keep himself from falling asleep.
Someone wrote a book just before being beheaded.
Someone was enlightened on his death bed.
Someone gave his body to the hungry tigers.
Someone faced the hunter's arrow to save a mother deer.*
Some of those are stories of the Buddha in earlier lives.
*And they all sacrificed their lives in loving kindness for sentient beings.

Ah, such a monk is not fit to live in this world.

Repeating such thoughts again and again, I took off my cloth and became stark naked.*
It's offering itself.
*I sat cross-legged on the deck, then hurried into the Samadhi, which scriptures call the Waveless Great Sea.
In the beginning, I still noticed the hum of the mosquitoes, but as time advanced, I forgot the heat, I forgot the hunger and thirst, and at last forgot the mosquitoes.
Waking and sleeping were about the same to me.
My mind was transparent.
I was flying in the utmost skies of emptiness.
I emptied the utmost Samadhi and felt the utmost contentment.
